source.title_on_document: Examining Human-AI Collaboration for Co-Writing Constructive Comments Online

supplement.where: Appendix A, pp. 30-33, Tables 11-20 and Figure 7. No external supplement identified.
supplement.holds: Thread titles, model settings and prompts; Table 13 stimulus validation; Table 14 perceived features; Table 15 between-source tests; Tables 16 and 18 length-adjusted ANCOVAs; Table 17 initial/final tests; Table 19 country-specific linguistic values; Table 20 writing-experience tests. Exact U/W/F statistics, p thresholds, and r/η² effects are included; no SE or CI is supplied for the core diversity comparison.

paper_design_summary: Indian and US crowd workers first validated and evaluated GPT-4 comments; a separate randomized experiment assigned people to independent writing or GPT-4 rewriting of their drafts (pp. 7-12). The writing experiment reports 103 analyzed/completing writers, with constructiveness, linguistic features, and cross-writer similarity scored on their comments; separate raters also compared AI-only and human-only comments (pp. 12, 14-19). Core evidence comes from the randomized writing comparison.

studies.label: Phase 1 preparatory validation of GPT-4 argumentation styles

assignment.what_was_assigned: Random selection of threads and GPT-4 comments for annotation, including random stances for neutral annotators. No assignment of AI help for human writing.
assignment.quote: Then, we showed them either one randomly selected homophobic or Islamophobic thread, along with four randomly selected LLM-generated comments written for that thread.
assignment.prereg_locator: Not stated in full text or Appendix A (pp. 1-33).

arms.name: Dialectical comments
arms.description: GPT-4 dialectical argumentation shown as annotation stimuli, not assistance.

participants.exclusions: Participant exclusions not stated. Incorrectly classified comments and comments without sufficient agreement were regenerated (p. 8).
participants.who: MTurk annotators: US 142, India 88 (p. 9, Table 2). These people rated stimuli; they did not write creative outputs.
participants.quote: we conducted a validation study with 230 crowd workers from MTurk in India and the US.

ai_tool.name_model: GPT-4; exact model snapshot not stated
ai_tool.how_used: Researchers generated logical and dialectical comments using country and stance prompts; model settings and prompts appear on pp. 30-31, Table 12.

studies.label: Phase 2: randomized comment writing with or without GPT-4

assignment.what_was_assigned: People were assigned to independent writing or GPT-4 rewriting of their drafts. Thread and prompt orders were randomized. Initial/final comparisons within the test group are ancillary before/after analyses, not another randomized contrast.
assignment.quote: We designed a between-subjects experiment where participants were randomly assigned to either a control or a test group.
assignment.locator: p. 10, Section 3.2, Writing Task; p. 11 for prompt order.
assignment.prereg_locator: Not stated in full text or Appendix A (pp. 1-33).

arms.name: HAI-written comments (test)
arms.description: People drafted their response and requested GPT-4 rewriting; suggestions could be accepted, edited, rejected, or regenerated. 102 comments are reported; the analyzed number of people in this arm is not explicitly stated (pp. 11-12).

arms.name: Human-written comments (control)
arms.description: People wrote without external assistance, including the Internet or ChatGPT. 104 comments are reported; the analyzed number of people in this arm is not explicitly stated (pp. 10, 12).

participants.exclusions: The introduction reports 103 writers (p. 2); Table 5 reports US 52 and India 51 completers (p. 12). Recruitment instead reports 52 Indian and 52 American recruits (p. 12). The reason for the difference is not stated. Recruitment counts are not explicitly assignment counts, so n_randomized is null. Arm-specific people counts are not inferred from comments. The reference to 87 participants incorporating suggestions on p. 16 has an unresolved denominator/unit and is not used as an independent people count.
participants.who: Prolific writers distinct from Phase 1. Separate raters in S4 are not included in the writer count.
participants.quote: with a different set of 103 Indian and American crowd workers on Prolific.
participants.locator: p. 2, Introduction; p. 12, Section 3.2, Participant Recruitment and Table 5.

ai_tool.name_model: GPT-4; exact model snapshot not stated
ai_tool.how_used: People wrote at least 20 words before requesting AI rewriting. They selected provided or custom prompts for relevance, logic, solutions, balanced viewpoints, or politeness. GPT-4 received the thread, country, stance, and draft. The test group had to prompt it at least once and could accept, reject, regenerate, or edit suggestions before final submission (pp. 10-11, Section 3.2, Figure 2).

task.description: Write one constructive English comment on a homophobic thread and one on an Islamophobic thread relevant to the writer's country, expressing their own stance. Final comments had to be at least 50 words. This task is in scope through similarity across writers, not an explicit originality rating (pp. 6, 10-12, 17-19).
task.duration: No fixed limit stated. Mean writing time: test 5.17 minutes; control 6.71 minutes (p. 16, Section 4.2.1).

outcomes.name: Semantic similarity across writers
outcomes.question: across_people
outcomes.measure_detail: Methods specify all-MiniLM-L6-v2 on p. 12; Section 4.2.3 applies semantic similarity to different writers (pp. 17-18). This is distinct from draft-final similarity within one writer. No outcome is explicitly designated primary.

contrasts.reported: Control 0.41; test 0.42. Table 8 prints a dash under statistics, and the text reports no significant difference. No SD, SE, exact p-value, or test statistic is printed.
contrasts.locator: pp. 17-18, Section 4.2.3; p. 18, Table 8.

diversity_detail.metric: Semantic similarity; higher raw scores mean lower diversity.
diversity_detail.computed_over: Different writers within the same arm, on the same thread and sharing the same stance (p. 17, Section 4.2.3). Pair enumeration, aggregation, and number of pairs are not stated.
diversity_detail.uncertainty: Mann-Whitney U tests with Bonferroni corrections (p. 18, Table 8). No participant-clustered uncertainty, bootstrap, SE, or CI is reported; exact dependence handling is not described.
diversity_detail.notes: Raw similarity would require sign reversal for the atlas diversity direction. No effect is computed here. The vocabulary has no means-only category: statistics_available none indicates absent precision/test statistics, not absent arm averages.

outcomes.name: Human-rated constructiveness: AI-assisted versus independent comments
outcomes.question: with_ai
outcomes.measure_detail: Separate Prolific raters chose the more constructive same-thread, same-stance comment. There were 401 HAI-versus-Human pair evaluations in the S4 rating dataset; pair here means one rated pair, not necessarily a unique pair. Constructiveness is output quality, not an explicit creativity score. Chi-square N=802 is not a people count. No participant-level or rater-clustered uncertainty is stated (pp. 12, 14-15).

contrasts.reported: HAI preferred in 64% versus Human in 36%; χ²(1, N=802)=62.56, p<0.000005, φ=0.28, odds ratio=3.19. India: HAI 66% versus Human 34%, χ²(1, N=205)=39.96, p<0.000005, φ=0.31. US: HAI 62% versus Human 38%, χ²(1, N=392)=22.54, p<0.000005, φ=0.24. Indian N is transcribed as printed and requires clarification.
contrasts.locator: p. 14, Section 4.2.1 for 401 pair evaluations; p. 15, Table 6, Figure 4, and Section 4.2.1.

outcomes.name: Lexical overlap across writers: cosine similarity and ROUGE-L
outcomes.question: across_people
outcomes.measure_detail: Grouped lexical-overlap variants: cosine similarity of CountVectorizer word-count vectors (p. 12) and ROUGE-L longest common subsequence (pp. 17-18). Cosine here is not an embedding measure. Table 8 spells ROUGE-L as Rogue-L.

contrasts.reported: Cosine similarity: control 0.33, test 0.30; statistics column is a dash and text reports no significant difference. Rogue-L: control 0.18, test 0.16; U=42029, Z=-3.73, p<0.001, r=0.16. Raw overlap is lower with AI for both variants, but a significant difference is reported only for ROUGE-L. Lower overlap corresponds to higher diversity.
contrasts.locator: pp. 17-19, Section 4.2.3; p. 18, Table 8.

diversity_detail.metric: Cosine similarity of word-count vectors; ROUGE-L longest common subsequence.
diversity_detail.embedding_model: None: scikit-learn CountVectorizer for cosine (p. 12); no embedding model for ROUGE-L.
diversity_detail.computed_over: Different writers within the same arm, on the same thread and sharing the same stance (p. 17, Section 4.2.3). Pair enumeration, aggregation, and number of pairs are not stated.
diversity_detail.uncertainty: Mann-Whitney U tests with Bonferroni corrections (p. 18, Table 8). No participant-clustered uncertainty, bootstrap, SE, or CI is reported; exact dependence handling is not described.
diversity_detail.notes: Diversity direction reverses the raw overlap sign. Mixed denotes different statistical findings across variants, not opposite point-estimate directions.

outcomes.name: Lexical diversity: distinct-2 and type-token ratio
outcomes.question: across_people
outcomes.measure_detail: The paper presents distinct-2 and TTR as vocabulary-diversity checks under homogeneity; grouped as two variants of lexical diversity. Their formulas, aggregation, and per-comment versus pooled-corpus computation are not stated. Unit output is provisional from the description of diversity in comments, and needs confirmation before treating these as across-person diversity.

contrasts.locator: p. 18, Table 8; p. 19, first paragraph of Section 4.2.3.

diversity_detail.metric: Distinct-2 and type-token ratio; higher raw values mean greater vocabulary diversity.
diversity_detail.computed_over: HAI-written versus human-written comments. Exact within-comment, pair, or corpus computation is not specified (pp. 17-19, Section 4.2.3).
diversity_detail.uncertainty: Mann-Whitney U tests with Bonferroni corrections (p. 18, Table 8). No participant-clustered uncertainty, bootstrap, SE, or CI is reported; exact dependence handling is not described.
diversity_detail.notes: Provisional across_people coding follows the authors' homogeneity analysis; lexical richness within one comment would not itself measure diversity across writers. Do not use this ambiguous measure alone for eligibility. No sign reversal.

studies.label: Phase 2 independent evaluation: AI-only versus human-only comments

assignment.what_was_assigned: Random thread/comment selection and display order for separate raters, not assistance for writing. The AI-only versus human-only contrast uses researcher-generated comments and existing S3 control comments. This panel also supplied HAI-versus-Human scores recorded once in S3.
assignment.quote: Each participant saw each comment only in one pair and we randomized the order of comments within each pair.
assignment.locator: p. 12, Section 3.2, Human Evaluation of Constructiveness.
assignment.prereg_locator: Not stated in full text or Appendix A (pp. 1-33).

arms.name: AI-only comments
arms.description: Researcher-generated GPT-4 comments from Phase 1; no human was assisted in producing these.

arms.name: Human-only comments
arms.description: Existing independent-writing control comments from S3; not a new writer sample.

participants.exclusions: Recruited 82 Indian and 82 American raters; seven failed the attention check. The 157 analyzed raters provided 727 evaluations across all three comparison types. Distinct rater count for AI-only versus human-only specifically is not stated.
participants.who: Separate Prolific raters who had not participated in Phase 1 or the writing task. These are evaluators, not writers.
participants.quote: In total, we received 727 human evaluations from 157 participants after discarding responses from 7 participants, who failed the attention check.
participants.locator: p. 12, Section 3.2, Human Evaluation of Constructiveness; p. 14, Section 4.2.1.

ai_tool.name_model: GPT-4; exact model snapshot not stated
ai_tool.how_used: Researchers generated the AI-only comments. Evaluators received no AI help producing creative outputs.

task.description: Select the more constructive member of same-thread, same-stance comment pairs. HAI-versus-Human results from this panel are attached to S3, while this entry retains the AI-only versus human-only benchmark (pp. 12, 14-15).

outcomes.name: Human-rated constructiveness: AI-only versus human-only comments
outcomes.question: none
outcomes.measure_detail: Forced-choice output-quality judgment. The source reports 141 Human-versus-AI pair evaluations; pair denotes a rated pair, not necessarily a unique pair. χ² N=282 is not a people count. This benchmark does not estimate assistance to a human writer (pp. 14-15).

contrasts.reported: AI preferred in 74% versus Human in 26%; χ²(1, N=282)=65.59, p<0.000005, φ=0.48, odds ratio=8.51. India: AI 69% versus Human 31%, χ²(1, N=148)=19.70, p<0.000005, φ=0.36. US: AI 81% versus Human 19%, χ²(1, N=134)=47.76, p<0.000005, φ=0.60.

sample_overlap.shares_participants_with: No reuse of another paper's participants is stated. Within this paper S4 rates existing S3 outputs and Phase 1 AI comments; the HAI-versus-Human result is recorded once under S3. Writing and rating samples are described as distinct from preceding phases.

eligibility.reason: S3 randomly assigns people to GPT-4 assistance versus independent writing (p. 10, Section 3.2). The introduction reports 103 writers and Table 5 lists 52 US plus 51 Indian completers, exceeding 50 despite a recruitment discrepancy (pp. 2, 12). Cosine similarity, semantic similarity, and ROUGE-L compare different writers on the same thread and stance (pp. 17-19, Section 4.2.3, Table 8), meeting the codebook's inclusion of writing tasks compared across writers. AI was available during final-output production (pp. 10-11). Only S3 supports core eligibility; S4 adds an AI-only benchmark. Neither evaluator counts nor output counts are used to meet the writer-size criterion.

one_line_finding: Among 103 completing writers (pp. 2, 12, Table 5), AI-assisted comments had similar semantic similarity to control (0.42 versus 0.41) but lower ROUGE-L overlap (0.16 versus 0.18; U=42029, p<0.001, r=0.16; p. 18, Table 8).
open_questions: Why does recruitment report 52 Indian and 52 US writers, while Table 5 reports 51 Indian and 52 US completers and the introduction states 103? Exact assigned and arm-specific people counts are not stated (pp. 2, 12).
What is the unit and denominator of the 87 participants incorporating suggestions? Do not treat this as a verified count of independent test-arm people (pp. 10, 12, 16).
How were similarity scores aggregated and was repeated use of writers/comments accounted for? Table 8 gives no observation counts, SDs, SEs, CIs, or clustering (pp. 17-19).
Were distinct-2 and TTR computed per comment, per pair, or on pooled outputs? Their inclusion under homogeneity does not establish an across-person computation (pp. 17-19).

Evaluation methods specify four pairs per rater but report 727 evaluations from 157 raters; Table 6 also prints N=205 for Indian HAI-versus-Human evaluations. The units and discrepancy require clarification (pp. 12, 14-15).

The stimulus description reports 64 AI comments, 32 per country, whereas Table 2 reports 39 US and 32 Indian comments meeting validation. Selection from all validated comments is not fully described (pp. 8-9).
notes: Screened 2026-10-09. Entire markdown read (1074 lines, references and appendix included); coded quantities checked against PDF page text. PyMuPDF table extraction also checked Tables 8 and 15-17. All locators are 1-based PDF pages. No effect size or precision estimate computed. Four substantive independently recruited panels/datasets are retained: validation (S1), perception experiment (S2), writers (S3), and independent evaluation with an AI-only benchmark (S4). S4 reuses S3 outputs, and its HAI-versus-Human result appears only under S3. Largest analyzed panel is 230 validation raters; eligible writer sample is 103. The preliminary pilot providing questionnaire explanations (US 27, India 22; p. 10) is instrument development, not a separately reported outcome study.  Outcome inventory from figures/tables: Figure 3 and Table 14 report constructiveness preferences and reasons; Figures 4-5 and Tables 6, 15, 16, 19 report pairwise constructiveness and eight linguistic features (length, readability, politeness, named entities, discourse connectives, stance adverbials, reasoning verbs/modals, root clauses); Figure 6 and Tables 17-18 report draft-final content similarity, sentiment, toxicity, and those linguistic features; Table 8 reports cosine similarity, semantic similarity, ROUGE-L, distinct-2, and TTR; Table 13 reports features of AI-only logical/dialectical stimuli. Section 4.2.4 additionally reports manually identified changes of opinion and sentiment/toxicity after editing. Time to write (pp. 16, 20), prompts and suggestion actions (Tables 7, 10; pp. 16, 19), and satisfaction, ownership, and difficulty (Tables 9, 20) are process/self-report measures, not scored creative outputs. The form retains 15 outcome entries. Cosine and ROUGE-L are grouped lexical-overlap variants; distinct-2 and TTR are grouped lexical-diversity variants; length-adjusted and country analyses remain with their original feature. Under the outcome cap, omitted as separate entries are initial-to-final content retention (semantic similarity, BERTScore, cosine similarity; pp. 16-18, Figure 6A) and manual changes in users' opinions (p. 19, Section 4.2.4). Neither is diversity across people. AI-only linguistic benchmarks and logical/dialectical stimulus comparisons are not repeated as outcome entries (pp. 31-32, Tables 13, 15); these do not answer the three AI-assistance questions. HAI-versus-AI constructiveness is also not a separate entry: Table 6 reports no significant difference; the p. 15 prose reports AI preferred in 55%, whereas Figure 4 gives 56%, and this is not silently reconciled. There is no unassisted post-AI task. Initial drafts precede assistance, and final outputs are produced while AI remains available; within-test before/after contrasts are not after_ai and are not randomized contrasts. Table 8 cross-writer diversity is distinct from Figure 6A within-writer content retention. No preregistration or study data/code release URL is stated; generic software documentation on p. 12 is not study data/code. S1 and S2 have no outcomes answering the three atlas questions; randomized stimulus display does not make them AI-assistance RCTs, and human-versus-GPT-4 judgments are not AI-versus-human writing.
